Consult Summary:
45-year-old female hotel housekeeper with 3–4 months of painful, itchy, cracked palmar skin most consistent with irritant contact dermatitis related to occupational chemical exposure.

History:
• Chief complaint: Painful fissuring and marked dryness of both palms; intermittent itch.  
• Onset & course: Began 3–4 months ago after starting a new housekeeping job; progressively worsened, now severe enough to miss the last 3 workdays.  
• Exacerbating factors: Likely exposure to cleaning products; patient “not always very good about wearing gloves.”  
• Relieving factors/attempted therapies: OTC E45 emollient (no benefit); unspecified antihistamine (no benefit).  
• Associated symptoms: Occasional bleeding only after scratching; mild generalized leg dryness.  
• Pertinent negatives: No fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary changes; appetite intact.

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus (duration not specified; complications not discussed).  
• No known prior skin disorders (denies eczema or dermatitis).

Medications:
• Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• OTC E45 emollient cream – as needed.  
• Unspecified antihistamine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  

Allergies:
• No known drug or other allergies.

Social History:
• Occupation: Hotel housekeeper; frequent contact with cleaning agents; inconsistent glove use.  
• Tobacco: Never smoker.  
• Alcohol: ~2 pints beer per week.  
• Recent work impact: Missed 3 days due to hand pain.

Family History:
• Diabetes mellitus.  
• No known dermatologic, asthma, or bowel disease.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded.  
• Skin (patient-reported via tele-visit): Palms very dry with cracking/fissures; intermittent itch; occasional scratch-induced bleeding.  
• Other systems: Not recorded.

Investigations:
• None ordered or reviewed during this visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Occupational irritant contact dermatitis of the palms, likely from cleaning chemicals.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Irritant contact dermatitis – strong temporal link to chemical exposure, predominant pain/fissures, no prior atopy.  
2. Allergic contact dermatitis – possible given occupational allergens; itch present but pain/fissures predominate.  
3. Chronic hand (atopic) eczema – less likely; no personal/family atopy, clear occupational trigger.

Issue 1: Palmar dermatitis  
• Assessment: Suspected irritant contact dermatitis.  
• Plan:  
  – Strict avoidance of triggers; wear protective gloves at all times while cleaning.  
  – Prescribe medium-potency topical corticosteroid cream (specific agent/dose not documented during call).  
  – Prescribe heavier emollient; apply generously 3–4 times daily for 2 weeks.  
  – Education on skin care, hand protection, and early signs of infection.  
  – Follow-up: Re-evaluate in 1–2 weeks; sooner if worsening, spreading, or signs of infection.

Issue 2: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (background)  
• Assessment: Stable; no discussion of glycemic control.  
• Plan: Continue current metformin; routine diabetes follow-up with primary care/provider as scheduled.

General plan items:  
• Prescription sent electronically to patient’s pharmacy.  
• Advised to return earlier if condition deteriorates or interferes further with work.

Quality checks:
● Missing clinically expected elements: vitals, full skin examination, diabetes control parameters, medication dosages.  
● No transcript–DDx conflicts noted.  
● Transcript quality adequate (minimal inaudible segments).
